chapter: The Pelican band and Ridgley years
title: Pensacola band breaks up and Sayles returns to join Bebe Ridgley's Pelican band
summary: Eagle Eye hires Edmund Hall away, Albert Morgan goes home with Sam Morgan, Sayles returns to New Orleans c. 1927 and joins Ridgley's Pelican Roof band with David Jones directing.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money

blocks.x: Did you ever hear Alonzo Ross? Alonzo Ross. Alonzo Ross, he was a piano player I think over there. From where? Around Jacksonville, I think.

Well, I probably met him, a lot of the guys. He went to New York. Yeah. Well, that happened years later because now I want to get, you still get on that same kick in Jacksonville. Now, Eagle Eyes had came out somewhere and heard our band. In fact, we even went up and sat in with the band. And he liked me, who I played bands, he liked the way Alvin Morgan played the bass, and he liked the way Edmund Hall played his playing and sax. And he wanted us to quit the band. That we had always promised that we would come back to Pensacola, you see. So, I can say this, yeah, we did made our way back. We came on back to Pensacola. And our famous town was, after Pensacola, was Mobile. We always knew we could be good, but we still had that big rep, you see, around Mobile. And I remember coming back, after our first trip coming back to Pensacola, and our first trip going to Mobile, and the first trip coming back to the Mobile, Evan Hall had got a wire from this guy, Eagle Eyes. And Albert Morgan, I think, Sam Morgan was coming to Mobile kind of regularly then, and we had left Pensacola and come to Mobile this day, you see. And, well, Pope and them being a union band, we wasn't in the union, well, they made it kind of hard for us around there, you see. And we didn't do so well around there. So, first I think it was Edmund Hall left. He told me, come to me, and Albert, he said, I got this office, I'm going to save you, do y'all want to go? So, Albert was kind of discouraged. He was talking about his brother wanted to take him back home, you know, which Albert Morgan did leave there. Sam Morgan took him back to New Orleans, and I stayed around there. And, uh, uh, Edmund Hall kept on talking to me about this deal, so, it seemed that while he was in talking to me, he was looking, because he wanted, that's why he had his eyes on Cootie. So, I was on two points myself, I said, well, it looked like things ain't getting so good. Well, I really didn't want to leave the band, because the fellas had actually given me my first break, and they had a lot of hopes in me, you see. I mean, especially George Washington and Mack, you know what I mean, you see. George who? George, I mean, George Morris. That was the time I was playing. Yeah. So, like I said, we wasn't doing so well, and so, the time was coming close for Edmund Hall, he either had to take me, or he either take somebody else. So, he went and took the other guy, which was working with Homer's band, named Frank. I believe his name is Frank Jack. He took him on banjo, and he took Cootie and himself, and he, I mean, Edmund, I remember the time he had a Dodge car, and he took the, his woman, Miss Irene, and they drove to Jacksonville. And I didn't see Edmund no more, and I stayed around there a while yet, and I eventually told you all, I said, well, I think I'd best be going, I came on back home, you see. And when I came back here, I had written to my dad about a month before I was coming back, you see. Because I didn't want to put the fellas down. We had some few dates, and I went and played with them, because we used to play a lot of those out of town movies. I remember one time named Pritchett, and a couple other places, I can't think of the name. We played, but the whole of them had really got hard on us, because, apart from not being a union band and staying there, they really made it hard, because we made it, and we was taking work out of them out, you see. So like I say, I left from there, and I came back here, and we were still living up on Rampart, yeah, I believe we were still living on Rampart 360, 20, 20, I think we were still living up there, yeah. Well, anyhow, my daddy had an all-in-range with me to work with B.B. Risley had broke up the Tuxedo band, him and Celestane had fell out, and he had a group, and Celestane had a group. And B.B. Risley had the job on the Pelican, and his brother was running the Pelican for fallback, and it was a beautiful place. And so I went down in a rehearsal with him one night, and I had a fellow named Willie Bonte, I'd be playing banjo with him. And at that same time, they had originally had asked me about Alfred Morgan, and Alfred Morgan was already in time, I think he was playing with Rene, he had got him a job. Because I mean, like I said, a good musician, when you're a good musician, you get around, people know you, and you can play, and you know, you'll always get your job. So he had wanted to change bass on, you know, did I ever wake up there? Yeah, he did wake up there a while. He always wanted to change, you know, so I said, yeah, I was a good musician. I said, I've just been playing with Rene, and so Al would wait for us a while. And then David Jones came. David Jones had been here, I believe, I hadn't known him. So he got David Jones. But David Jones had told himself that he had went up, when he came here, he went up to the guy to try to get in the roof garden. Well, he couldn't get in that band, because they had been together so long. Willie Humphrey had been in there with Manuel Perez, and Capri, and that same group, they had been again a long time, you see. And then he, some kind of way, he picked up on B'Bare, really. So he got in the band. Well, the band already had, they had Robert Hall, and they had another fellow named Joe Watson, that was a very good saxophone and clarinet player. That was two, yeah. And Schatz was already in that band. They had another trumpet player named, and he was a little black and white fellow. He used to be a prize fighter. I don't know what that fellow's name. He's out in El Paso now. Bat Brown, had him on trumpet. And Emma Bauer on piano. And I believe he had Happy, yeah, Happy Playing Drum. Happy Playing Drum. So we, that band, built up to be a pretty good band on the Pelican, because we would rehearse and we would get good arrangement down through the direction of David John. David John had charge of what they called being the director and leader of the band. And we would take, buy the stock numbers and take them and change them around. And David John had a good idea of, he could write music and he could give a man a note. He could take his sax section and say, you take this note and this note, he'd take the brass section and say, you all take this note and this note. And he had already had experience playing with Fred Marl for years back, which you remember reading in history. So we built up a great band up there. They used to call us the Great Pelican Band. And they used to have, in them days they used to have what they called, the nights they'd have two bands. In other words, there was a book between the roof guard and the pelican in those days. And I had went back to, I had brought my violin back to Pensacola. I forgot to tell you about that. But I eventually got away from violin, so they knew how I played violin. So I used to bring my violin, a couple of them I used to play on the walls, you know, but I had kind of just got, because I found there wasn't no money. Most things wasn't no money to me, but playing the violin, you see. And so I think why I say I stuck most to playing the banjo. Now, as I said, oh yeah.
